claim: The human gut microbiota impacts host metabolism and has been implicated in the pathophysiology of obesity and metabolic syndromes.
source: The human gut microbiota impacts host metabolism and has been implicated in the pathophysiology of obesity and metabolic syndromes.
evidence: This is a general statement about established knowledge in the field, supported by the broader scientific literature.

claim: Strains from the abundant gut bacterial phylum Bacteroidetes display selective bile salt hydrolase (BSH) activity.
source: Here, we identify strains from the abundant gut bacterial phylum Bacteroidetes that display selective bile salt hydrolase (BSH) activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2A showing differential BSH activity across Bacteroidetes strains.

claim: B. thetaiotaomicron BSH mutant-colonized mice displayed altered metabolism, including reduced weight gain and respiratory exchange ratios.
source: B. thetaiotaomicron BSH mutant-colonized mice displayed altered metabolism, including reduced weight gain and respiratory exchange ratios, as well as transcriptional changes in metabolic, circadian rhythm, and immune pathways in the gut and liver.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5A and 6A demonstrating reduced weight gain and altered RER in BSH mutant-colonized mice.

claim: Metabolites generated by a single microbial gene and enzymatic activity can profoundly alter host metabolism and gene expression at local and organism-level scales.
source: Our results demonstrate that metabolites generated by a single microbial gene and enzymatic activity can profoundly alter host metabolism and gene expression at local and organism-level scales.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data showing that deletion of BT2086 affects bile acid pools, host metabolism, and gene expression.

claim: The human gut microbiome plays a crucial role in human energy harvest and homeostasis.
source: The human gut microbiome is known to play a crucial role in human energy harvest and homeostasis (BäckhedBackhed et al., 2004; Turnbaugh et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Lean and obese people harbor different gut bacterial communities.
source: Lean and obese people harbor different gut bacterial communities, suggesting that developing gut bacterial imbalances may contribute to obesity (Ley et al., 2006; Turnbaugh et al., 2006; Turnbaugh et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Transplantation of the fecal microbiota from obese humans to germ-free mice results in the development of obesity-associated metabolic phenotypes in recipient mice.
source: Importantly, transplantation of the fecal microbiota from obese humans to germ-free (GF) mice has been shown to result in the development of obesity-associated metabolic phenotypes in recipient mice (Ridaura et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: There is a causal relationship between gut bacteria and host metabolic status.
source: These studies establish a causal relationship between gut bacteria and host metabolic status.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited transplantation studies.

claim: The molecular mechanisms by which gut microbes regulate host metabolism remain largely unknown.
source: The molecular mechanisms by which gut microbes regulate host metabolism, however, remain largely unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Some bacterial metabolites accumulate to levels in the body higher than that of a typical drug.
source: One of the most concrete effects that human-associated bacteria have on the host is the production of small molecule metabolites, some of which accumulate to levels in the body higher than that of a typical drug (Donia and Fischbach, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Bacterial metabolites play important roles in host metabolism by regulating host glucose and energy homeostasis.
source: Recent research suggests that bacterial metabolites play important roles in host metabolism by regulating host glucose and energy homeostasis (De Vadder et al., 2014; Gao et al., 2009; Todesco et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Bile acids are steroidal natural products that are synthesized from cholesterol in the liver.
source: Bile acids are steroidal natural products that are synthesized from cholesterol in the liver and constitute an important part of the molecular environment of a healthy human gut (Ridlon et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Approximately 3–5% of bile acids escape enterohepatic recirculation and enter the colon at a rate of 400–800 mg/day.
source: Approximately 3–5% of bile acids escape enterohepatic recirculation and enter the colon at a rate of 400–800 mg/day, forming a concentrated pool of metabolites (200 to 1000 μM) (Hamilton et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: In the colon, bile acids are modified by resident bacteria in near-quantitative fashion, forming a class of on the order of 50 different metabolites called secondary bile acids.
source: In the colon, these molecules are modified by the resident bacteria in near-quantitative fashion, forming a class of on the order of 50 different metabolites called secondary bile acids (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Many primary and secondary bile acids act as ligands for host nuclear receptors, including FXR, PXR, VDR, LXR and TGR5.
source: In addition to their role in digestion, many primary and secondary bile acids act as ligands for host nuclear receptors, including the farnesoid X receptor (FXR), the pregnane X receptor (PXR), the vitamin D receptor (VDR), the liver X receptor (LXR) and the G-protein-coupled receptor TGR5 (Fiorucci and Distrutti, 2015; Katsuma et al., 2005; Makishima et al., 2002; Song et al., 2000; Staudinger et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Bile acids impact the regulation of glucose tolerance and homeostasis, insulin sensitivity, lipid metabolism, triglyceride and cholesterol levels, and energy expenditure by the host.
source: By acting as agonists or antagonists for these receptors, bile acids further impact the regulation of glucose tolerance and homeostasis, insulin sensitivity, lipid metabolism, triglyceride and cholesterol levels, and energy expenditure by the host (Fiorucci and Distrutti, 2015; Modica et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Bile acids regulate their own biosynthesis via an FXR-mediated negative feedback mechanism.
source: Additionally, bile acids regulate their own biosynthesis via an FXR-mediated negative feedback mechanism, which affects downstream nutrient availability for the host (Modica et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Bile acid imbalance has been implicated as having a causal effect in the development of diet-induced obesity.
source: As a result of these interactions, bile acid imbalance has been implicated as having a causal effect in the development of diet-induced obesity (Fiorucci and Distrutti, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Modification of the bile acid pool by commensal bacteria has been suggested to induce beneficial changes in host metabolism.
source: Conversely, modification of the bile acid pool by commensal bacteria has been suggested to induce beneficial changes in host metabolism (Joyce et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: BSH hydrolyze conjugated bile acids that have been linked to either taurine or glycine by host liver enzymes, revealing unconjugated bile acids.
source: BSH hydrolyze conjugated bile acids that have been linked to either taurine or glycine by host liver enzymes, revealing unconjugated bile acids (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: BSH deconjugation occurs prior to subsequent bacterial conversion of primary bile acids to secondary bile acids.
source: This deconjugation step occurs prior to subsequent bacterial conversion of primary bile acids (e.g. cholic acid and chenodeoxycholic acid) to secondary bile acids (e.g. deoxycholic acid and lithocholic acid) (Ridlon et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: TCA is an FXR agonist.
source: TCA is an FXR agonist, while TβMCA is an FXR antagonist (Figure 1B) (Li et al., 2013; Sayin et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: TβMCA is an FXR antagonist.
source: TCA is an FXR agonist, while TβMCA is an FXR antagonist (Figure 1B) (Li et al., 2013; Sayin et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: BSH are found across a wide range of bacterial genera from the two dominant gut phyla, Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes.
source: BSH (EC 3.5.1.24) are found across a wide range of bacterial genera from the two dominant gut phyla, Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes (Jones et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The structural and activity characterization of BSH enzymes has been largely limited to Gram-positive species.
source: However, the structural and activity characterization of these enzymes has been largely limited to Gram-positive species (i.e. Clostridia, Lactobacillus, Bifidobacterium, Listeria) (Begley et al., 2006; Rossocha et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: BSH enzymes from Gram-positive species largely demonstrate non-selective activities, cleaving all conjugated bile acids independent of either the bile acid core or amino acid conjugate.
source: These enzymes largely demonstrate non-selective activities, cleaving all conjugated bile acids independent of either the bile acid core or amino acid conjugate (taurine or glycine) (Ridlon et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Bacteroides fragilis ATCC 25285 exhibits non-selective BSH activity.
source: While Bacteroides fragilis ATCC 25285 was reported to exhibit non-selective BSH activity (Stellwag and Hylemon, 1976), some Bacteroides vulgatus strains were observed to cleave taurochenodeoxycholic acid (TCDCA) and TβMCA but minimally cleaved TCA (Chikai et al., 1987; Kawamoto et al., 1989), thus exhibiting a degree of selectivity based on the hydroxylation pattern of the steroid.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Some Bacteroides vulgatus strains cleave TCDCA and TβMCA but minimally cleave TCA, exhibiting selectivity based on the hydroxylation pattern of the steroid.
source: While Bacteroides fragilis ATCC 25285 was reported to exhibit non-selective BSH activity (Stellwag and Hylemon, 1976), some Bacteroides vulgatus strains were observed to cleave taurochenodeoxycholic acid (TCDCA) and TβMCA but minimally cleaved TCA (Chikai et al., 1987; Kawamoto et al., 1989), thus exhibiting a degree of selectivity based on the hydroxylation pattern of the steroid.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: C. perfringens ATCC 13124, L. plantarum WCFS1, and B. fragilis ATCC 25285 deconjugated all conjugated bile acid substrates tested.
source: As expected, C. perfringens ATCC 13124, L. plantarum WCFS1, and B. fragilis ATCC 25285 deconjugated all conjugated bile acid substrates tested.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The majority of Bacteroidetes strains tested displayed some degree of selectivity for conjugated bile acid substrates, with a preference for deconjugating tauro- over glyco-conjugated substrates.
source: Strikingly, the majority of Bacteroidetes strains tested displayed some degree of selectivity for conjugated bile acid substrates, with a preference for deconjugating tauro- over glyco-conjugated substrates.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A subset of Bacteroidetes strains (Group I) exhibited selectivity exclusively based on the steroidal core structure, deconjugating C12 = H primary bile acids but not C12 = OH primary bile acids.
source: A subset of these strains (B. thetaiotaomicron VPI-5482, B. caccae ATCC 43185, B. fragilis 638R, Bacteroides sp. D2, and Bacteroides sp. 2_1_16; Group I – red, Figure 2A) exhibited selectivity exclusively based on the steroidal core structure, deconjugating C12 = H primary bile acids (i.e. TCDCA, GCDCA, and TβMCA) but not C12 = OH primary bile acids (i.e. TCA and GCA).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: BT2086 is responsible for bile salt hydrolase activity in B. thetaiotaomicron.
source: Complementation of the Bt KO strain with BT2086 restored BSH activity (Figure 2C), confirming that BT2086 is necessary for bile acid deconjugation in Bt.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C demonstrating loss and restoration of BSH activity.

claim: Bt wild-type deconjugates TβMCA but not TCA.
source: Finally, we verified that when incubated with both TβMCA and TCA, Bt wild-type (Bt WT) deconjugated TβMCA but not TCA, whereas the Bt KO strain did not deconjugate either bile acid (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The Bt KO strain does not deconjugate TβMCA or TCA.
source: Finally, we verified that when incubated with both TβMCA and TCA, Bt wild-type (Bt WT) deconjugated TβMCA but not TCA, whereas the Bt KO strain did not deconjugate either bile acid (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Preference for C12 = H over C12 = OH primary bile acid cores is an activity that may have evolved multiple times independently from related members of the BSH superfamily.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that preference for C12 = H over C12 = OH primary bile acid cores is an activity that may have evolved multiple times independently from related members of the BSH superfamily.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the phylogenetic analysis showing lack of clustering of Group I strains.

claim: Bt KO-colonized mice displayed higher levels of TβMCA in cecal contents than Bt WT-colonized mice.
source: As we predicted, Bt KO-colonized mice displayed higher levels of TβMCA in cecal contents than Bt WT-colonized mice in the monocolonization experiment (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Bt KO-colonized mice exhibited significantly lower levels of βMCA than Bt WT-colonized mice.
source: Bt KO-colonized mice also exhibited significantly lower levels of βMCA (p<0.0001), the product of TβMCA hydrolysis, than Bt WT-colonized mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The levels of TCA remained unchanged between Bt WT- and Bt KO-colonized mice.
source: Importantly, the levels of TCA remained unchanged between the two groups, and no CA was detected in either group.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: No CA was detected in either Bt WT- or Bt KO-colonized mice.
source: Importantly, the levels of TCA remained unchanged between the two groups, and no CA was detected in either group.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: GF mice had significantly higher overall bile acid levels than colonized mice.
source: In the CLAMS experiment, in agreement with previous reports (Sayin et al., 2013), GF mice had significantly higher overall bile acid levels than colonized mice (p=0.0012 Bt WT vs GF, p=0.0071 BT KO vs GF).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citation to previous research.

claim: Bt KO-colonized mice gained less weight on the high-fat diet than Bt WT-colonized mice.
source: Strikingly, Bt KO-colonized mice gained less weight on the high-fat diet than Bt WT-colonized mice in the monocolonization experiment (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: GF mice are more resistant to weight gain when fed a high-fat diet.
source: This result is notable because it has been shown that GF mice are more resistant to weight gain when fed a high-fat diet (Bäckhed et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Bt WT and Bt KO efficiently colonized the GI tract and remained the only bacterial species in the mono-associated animals.
source: Importantly, the host effects observed are not due to differences in colonization efficiency. In both experiments, Bt WT and Bt KO efficiently colonized the GI tract and remained the only bacterial species in the mono-associated animals (Figure 5B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Bt KO-colonized mice had lower levels of triglycerides, cholesterol, and free fatty acids in plasma compared to Bt WT-colonized mice.
source: Consistent with the reduced weight gain phenotype, we observed lower levels of triglycerides, cholesterol, and free fatty acids in plasma (Figure 5C) as well as lower triglyceride levels in liver (Figure 5D) of Bt KO-colonized compared to Bt WT-colonized mice in the monocolonization experiment.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: Bt KO-colonized mice had lower triglyceride levels in liver compared to Bt WT-colonized mice.
source: Consistent with the reduced weight gain phenotype, we observed lower levels of triglycerides, cholesterol, and free fatty acids in plasma (Figure 5C) as well as lower triglyceride levels in liver (Figure 5D) of Bt KO-colonized compared to Bt WT-colonized mice in the monocolonization experiment.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Bt KO-colonized mice exhibited less liver steatosis than Bt WT-colonized mice.
source: Bt KO-colonized mice also exhibited less liver steatosis than Bt WT-colonized mice, consistent with the lower liver triglyceride levels in the former group (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Both Bt KO-colonized mice and GF mice displayed a lower respiratory exchange ratio (RER) than Bt WT-colonized mice.
source: Both Bt KO-colonized mice and GF mice displayed a lower respiratory exchange ratio (RER) than Bt WT-colonized mice (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Bt KO-colonized and GF mice are utilizing more lipids for energy than carbohydrates relative to Bt WT-colonized mice.
source: Thus, our data indicate that both the Bt KO-colonized and GF mice are utilizing more lipids for energy than carbohydrates relative to the Bt WT-colonized mice.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the RER data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Bt KO-colonized mice consumed more oxygen than Bt WT-colonized mice.
source: While Bt KO-colonized mice consumed more oxygen than Bt WT-colonized mice (Figure 6B), there were no significant differences in carbon dioxide production between groups (full day, Bt WT vs Bt KO p=0.4041; Bt WT vs GF p=0.3239; Bt KO vs GF p=0.0606) (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: There were no significant differences in carbon dioxide production between Bt WT-colonized, Bt KO-colonized, and GF mice.
source: While Bt KO-colonized mice consumed more oxygen than Bt WT-colonized mice (Figure 6B), there were no significant differences in carbon dioxide production between groups (full day, Bt WT vs Bt KO p=0.4041; Bt WT vs GF p=0.3239; Bt KO vs GF p=0.0606) (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Bt WT-colonized mice displayed a positive linear correlation between energy expenditure and body mass.
source: While Bt WT-colonized mice displayed this linear relationship (p=0.0168, R2 = 0.7134), strikingly, both Bt KO-colonized (p=0.6806, R2 = 0.03017) and GF (p=0.6930, R2 = 0.02782) mice did not (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Both Bt KO-colonized and GF mice did not display a linear relationship between energy expenditure and body mass.
source: While Bt WT-colonized mice displayed this linear relationship (p=0.0168, R2 = 0.7134), strikingly, both Bt KO-colonized (p=0.6806, R2 = 0.03017) and GF (p=0.6930, R2 = 0.02782) mice did not (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The deletion of a single bacterial gene, a selective bile salt hydrolase, results in loss of the relationship between metabolic rate and body weight in the host.
source: These data suggest that the deletion of a single bacterial gene, a selective bile salt hydrolase, results in loss of the relationship between metabolic rate and body weight in the host.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the regression analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Bt KO-colonized mice consumed less food during HFD feeding than Bt WT-colonized mice.
source: In the monocolonization experiment, Bt KO-colonized mice consumed less food during HFD feeding than Bt WT-colonized mice (−2.28 g ± 1.36 g vs. +3.39 g±1.61 g per cage per week, respectively, compared to weekly average for all cages, p=0.0165).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from food consumption measurements.

claim: There were no differences in solubilization of fats by bile acid pools from Bt KO- and Bt WT-colonized mice at 5 hr and 24 hr time points.
source: At both 5 hr and 24 hr time points, we did not detect any differences in solubilization at four different fat concentrations as measured by the turbidity of the resulting mixtures (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The metabolic differences observed between Bt WT- and Bt KO-colonized mice are not due to different detergent abilities of the bile acid pools.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that the metabolic differences observed between the Bt WT- and Bt KO-colonized mice are not due to different detergent abilities of the bile acid pools.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the detergent assay data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Fecal bomb calorimetry did not reveal any differences in energy remaining in fecal pellets from Bt WT-colonized, Bt KO-colonized, or GF mice.
source: In further support of this conclusion, fecal bomb calorimetry did not reveal any differences in energy remaining in fecal pellets from Bt WT-colonized, Bt KO-colonized, or GF mice, indicating that there were no notable differences in caloric energy extraction from food between these groups (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The observed metabolic differences between Bt WT- and Bt KO-colonized mice may be due to differences in bile acids acting as signaling molecules in the host.
source: These data suggest that the observed metabolic differences between Bt WT- and Bt KO-colonized mice may be due to differences in bile acids acting as signaling molecules in the host.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the detergent assay and calorimetry data.

claim: 428 genes were differentially expressed between Bt KO- and Bt WT-colonized mice in the distal ileum.
source: Global transcriptional analysis of the distal ileum identified 12,432 genes, of which 428 genes were differentially expressed (adjusted FDR ≤ 0.05, fold-change ≥±1.5) between the Bt KO- and Bt WT-colonized mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data analysis.

claim: The majority (314 genes) of differentially expressed genes were increased in Bt KO-colonized mice.
source: Of those genes, the majority (314 genes) were increased in the Bt KO-colonized mice (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The two monocolonized groups segregate based on their transcriptional profiles.
source: Multidimensional scaling analysis (MDS) revealed that the two monocolonized groups segregate based on their transcriptional profiles (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by MDS analysis shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Gene Ontology and KEGG pathway analyses revealed coordinated changes in gene expression related to metabolism, circadian rhythm, immune response, and histone modifications.
source: Gene Ontology (GO) and KEGG pathway analyses of RNA-Seq expression data revealed coordinated changes in gene expression related to metabolism, circadian rhythm, immune response, and histone modifications (Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by pathway analysis of RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Genes involved in the transport and breakdown of glucose were upregulated in Bt KO-colonized mice.
source: In particular, genes involved in the transport (Slc2a1) and breakdown (Hk1/2, Pfkl/m) of glucose were upregulated, whereas G6pc (glucose-6-phosphatase), the final enzyme in the gluconeogenesis pathway, was significantly downregulated (8.8-fold), indicating a shift away from gluconeogenesis and toward glycolysis in the distal ileum of Bt KO-colonized mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data analysis.

claim: G6pc was significantly downregulated (8.8-fold) in the distal ileum of Bt KO-colonized mice.
source: In particular, genes involved in the transport (Slc2a1) and breakdown (Hk1/2, Pfkl/m) of glucose were upregulated, whereas G6pc (glucose-6-phosphatase), the final enzyme in the gluconeogenesis pathway, was significantly downregulated (8.8-fold), indicating a shift away from gluconeogenesis and toward glycolysis in the distal ileum of Bt KO-colonized mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data analysis.

claim: Bt KO-colonized mice had significantly higher blood glucose levels compared to Bt WT-colonized mice.
source: Consistent with these findings, we observed significantly higher blood glucose levels in Bt KO-colonized mice compared to Bt WT-colonized mice in the CLAMS experiment (p=0.0228), indicating an increase in glucose available for glycolysis in the distal ileum (Figure 9A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Two key genes in the ketogenesis pathway, Bdh1 and Hmgcs2, were significantly upregulated in Bt KO-colonized mice.
source: Two key genes in the ketogenesis pathway, Bdh1 (3-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase 1) and Hmgcs2 (3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA synthase 2), were significantly upregulated (Figure 8C), indicating an increase in the use of lipid and ketogenic amino acid degradation for energy production in the host.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Pparg expression was significantly up-regulated in Bt KO-colonized mice.
source: RNA-Seq data revealed that Pparg expression was significantly up-regulated in Bt KO-colonized mice (Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 8C and confirmed by qPCR in Figure 8D.

claim: The observed inverse relationship between expression of transcriptional activators (Npas2 and Arntl) and circadian repressors (Per1, Per2, Per3, Cry2) is consistent with the transcription-translation negative feedback loop that establishes diurnal rhythms.
source: The observed inverse relationship between expression of the transcriptional activators (Npas2 and Arntl, decreased in Bt KO-colonized mice) and circadian repressors (Per1, Per2, Per3, Cry2, increased in Bt KO-colonized mice) is consistent with the transcription-translation negative feedback loop that establishes diurnal rhythms (King and Takahashi, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data and citation to previous research on circadian rhythm mechanisms.

claim: Tissues in the distal ileum of Bt KO-colonized mice exist in an altered circadian synchronization state compared to those of Bt WT-colonized mice.
source: These data indicate that tissues in the distal ileum of Bt KO-colonized mice exist in an altered circadian synchronization state compared to those of Bt WT-colonized mice.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the circadian gene expression data.

claim: Toll-like receptors (Tlr1, Tlr2, Tlr4) were significantly upregulated in Bt KO-colonized mice.
source: Of particular note, Toll-like receptors (Tlr1, Tlr2, Tlr4), innate immune receptors that play key roles in recognizing microbially produced molecules (Akira et al., 2001), were significantly upregulated in our Bt KO-colonized mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data analysis.

claim: Activation of ileal FXR leads to production of fibroblast growth factor 15/19 (FGF15 in mice and FGF19 in humans).
source: Specifically, activation of ileal FXR leads to production of fibroblast growth factor 15/19 (FGF15 in mice and FGF19 in humans).
evidence: This is established knowledge about FXR signaling pathways.

claim: FGF15 translocates to the liver where it binds to the FGFR4/β-Klotho complex and represses the expression of Cyp7a1.
source: FGF15 then translocates to the liver where it binds to the FGFR4/β-Klotho complex and represses the expression of Cyp7a1, which encodes an enzyme catalyzing the rate-limiting step in bile acid synthesis from cholesterol (Ding et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: No significant difference in FXR-dependent genes (Nr0b2/Shp, Fgf15, and Fabp6/Ibabp) was observed in the distal ileum between Bt KO- and Bt WT-colonized mice.
source: Contrary to our expectations, we did not observe a significant difference in genes downstream of FXR, including Nr0b2/Shp (p=0.2018), Fgf15 (p=0.6213), and Fabp6/Ibabp (p=0.6425), in the distal ileum (Figure 9B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: A downregulation of Nr0b2/Shp and upregulation of Cyp7a1 was observed in the liver of Bt KO-colonized mice.
source: We did observe a downregulation of Nr0b2/Shp and upregulation of Cyp7a1 in the liver of Bt KO-colonized mice, results that are consistent with increased TβMCA-mediated FXR antagonism in Bt KO-colonized mice (Figure 9C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: The total bile acid pool concentration in cecal contents was higher in Bt KO-colonized mice.
source: The total bile acid pool concentration in cecal contents was higher in Bt KO-colonized mice (Figure 4A), consistent with an increase in Cyp7a1 transcription resulting in an increase in bile acid synthesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by bile acid quantification data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The increase in G6pc in the liver of Bt KO-colonized mice is notable because this gene is significantly downregulated in the distal ilea of these mice.
source: The increase in G6pc in the liver of Bt KO-colonized mice is notable because this gene is significantly downregulated in the distal ilea of these mice (Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figures 8D and 9C.

claim: No significant differences in expression of Srebf1/Srebp1c, Fas, and Acc were observed between Bt KO- and WT-colonized mice.
source: No significant differences in expression of these genes, however, were observed between Bt KO- and WT-colonized mice (Srebf1/Srebp1c, p=0.5018; Fas, p=0.3292; Acaca, p=0.1302) (Figure 9C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Significant decreases in genes not known to be under the control of FXR, including Cd36, Tnf/Tnfα, Adgre1/Emr1, and Sphk2, were observed in the liver of Bt KO-colonized mice.
source: In addition, we observed significant decreases in genes not known to be under the control of FXR, including Cd36 (p=0.0015), a gene encoding a fatty acid transporter, the immune-related genes tumor necrosis factor alpha (Tnf/Tnfα, p=0.0225) and EGF-like module-containing mucin-like hormone receptor-like 1 (Adgre1/Emr1, p=0.0011), and the G-protein-coupled receptor S1pr2 target gene sphingosine kinase 2 (Sphk2, p=0.0274) (Nagahashi et al., 2015), in the liver of Bt KO-colonized mice (Figure 9C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Other host receptors may be involved in the transcriptional changes and metabolic differences observed.
source: These results indicate that other host receptors may be involved in the transcriptional changes and metabolic differences observed.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of FXR-independent gene expression changes.

claim: Changing the in vivo bile acid pool using selective expression of a bacterial bile salt hydrolase results in significant alterations in host gene expression.
